title: The Age of Exploration
subtitle: From Zheng He's fleets to the first voyage around the world, 1405 to 1522

steps.title: Zheng He's treasure fleet
steps.text: In 1405 the Yongle Emperor of Ming China sent the admiral Zheng He into the Indian Ocean with a great fleet assembled at Nanjing. It called at Champa, Java, Malacca, Sumatra and Ceylon and reached Calicut on the Malabar Coast. Six more voyages followed by 1433, some reaching Hormuz, Arabia and East Africa. Then the court ended them, for reasons still debated.

steps.title: Portugal takes Ceuta
steps.text: On 25 July 1415 a Portuguese fleet under King John I left Lisbon, rounded Cape St Vincent and paused at Lagos and Faro. On 21 August it captured Ceuta, on the African side of the Strait of Gibraltar. Prince Henry, aged 21, led troops ashore and was knighted there. The conquest is often taken as the beginning of the Portuguese Empire.

steps.title: Past Cape Bojador
steps.text: In 1434 Gil Eanes of Lagos, sent by Prince Henry, became the first known European to sail past Cape Bojador on the Saharan coast. An attempt the year before had failed. By 1444 Dinis Dias had rounded Cap-Vert, and by 1462 the Portuguese had explored the coast as far as present-day Sierra Leone. The famous school of navigation at Sagres is a later legend.

steps.title: Dias rounds Africa
steps.text: Bartolomeu Dias left Lisbon around July 1487 and worked south along the African coast. After about thirty days on the open ocean he passed the southern tip of the continent and entered Mossel Bay on 4 February 1488. He turned back at Kwaaihoek on 12 March. Tradition says he named the Cape of Storms, and that King John II renamed it the Cape of Good Hope.

steps.title: Columbus crosses the Atlantic
steps.text: Christopher Columbus sailed from Palos on 3 August 1492 with the Santa María, the Pinta and the Niña, backed by Ferdinand and Isabella. After a stop in the Canaries he crossed the Atlantic in five weeks and landed on 12 October on an island its people called Guanahani, in the Bahamas. He went on to Cuba and Hispaniola, sure he had reached the Indies.

steps.title: A line down the ocean
steps.text: On 7 June 1494, at Tordesillas in Spain, Castile and Portugal divided the newly found lands between them. They fixed a line from pole to pole 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands: lands to the east for Portugal, lands to the west for Castile. A papal bull the year before had set it only 100 leagues out. In 1529 the Treaty of Zaragoza added a second line near the Moluccas.

steps.title: Da Gama reaches India
steps.text: Vasco da Gama left Lisbon on 8 July 1497 with four ships and 170 men. He swung out into the open Atlantic past the Cape Verde Islands, rounded southern Africa, and worked up the east coast to Malindi, where he hired a pilot. On 20 May 1498 he reached Kappad, near Calicut, and Europe had a sea road to India. Only about 55 of his men came home.

steps.title: Cabral sights Brazil
steps.text: Pedro Álvares Cabral left Lisbon on 9 March 1500 with 13 ships and about 1,500 men, bound for India. On 22 April the fleet anchored off an unknown coast far to the west, near a hill he named Monte Pascoal, and two days later at Porto Seguro. He called the country the Island of the True Cross; it was Brazil. He then sailed on to Calicut.

steps.title: Balboa sees the South Sea
steps.text: On 25 September 1513 Vasco Núñez de Balboa climbed to a summit in Darién, on the Isthmus of Panama, and saw open water on the horizon. He named it the South Sea, because his expedition had marched south to reach it. It was a second ocean, lying beyond the lands Columbus had found. Seven years later Magellan gave it the name Pacific.

steps.title: Magellan finds the strait
steps.text: Ferdinand Magellan sailed from Sanlúcar de Barrameda on 20 September 1519 with five ships and about 270 men, in the service of Charles I of Spain. He wintered at Port St Julian in Patagonia, where he put down a mutiny, and lost one ship to wreck. On 1 November 1520 he entered the strait that bears his name. On 28 November he came out into the Pacific.

steps.title: Across the Pacific to Mactan
steps.text: The Pacific crossing took about 98 days. The fleet reached Guam on 6 March 1521 and Homonhon in the Philippines on 16 March, then Limasawa and Cebu, whose ruler was baptized. On 27 April Magellan attacked the nearby island of Mactan with about 60 men. The warriors of the chief Lapulapu overwhelmed them, and Magellan was killed on the beach.

steps.title: The Victoria comes home
steps.text: The survivors reached Tidore in the Moluccas on 8 November 1521. Juan Sebastián Elcano took one ship, the Victoria, west across the Indian Ocean and around Africa, touching at Cape Verde. On 6 September 1522 she anchored at Sanlúcar de Barrameda with 18 men aboard, out of about 270 who had set out. They were the first to sail around the world.
